parts: Lesson 31: Aesthetics at Home (Module 6A, lesson 31) — Summary

Cleaning includes putting things in a decided place; otherwise you waste time finding things and become unorganised. A cluttered house with unmatching curtains and too many decorations restricts movement; a good home has furniture in proportion to the room, well-arranged objects, curtains that give uniformity, pleasing colours, adequate lighting and free movement, so we feel rested and comfortable. Artistic touch makes things beautiful and comfortable.

Materials: vase (matching the surroundings; a small basket suits cane furniture and coir coverings), a pin holder (iron nails fixed on a heavy metal base, closely spaced, rust-free and long enough to hold stems) or oasis (absorbs a lot of water and keeps flowers moist; soak until bubbles stop; reusable 2–4 times; easier for beginners to balance flowers), fresh or artificial flowers, green leaves and twigs. Odd numbers of flowers (as few as three in ikebana, the Japanese art), of varying sizes. Twigs give a natural look; leaves fill gaps, give a background and make the arrangement resemble nature; wash dirty leaves and trim wilted ones.

Fix the pin holder to the container and pour water to cover it (or soak the oasis); decide the shape (triangle, right angle, oval, S-shape); choose flowers of different sizes; pluck flowers early in the morning and cut under water; cut stems at different lengths with the tallest at least 1½ times the width of the vase; arrange the tallest first and then the others in order of height, placing each branch firmly in the pin holder or oasis; put flowers at different heights with space between them, facing towards you; bigger flowers at the bottom, medium in the centre and buds at the top so it is not top-heavy; fill gaps with leaves of different sizes; hide the pin holder with leaves or stones; place against a contrasting background.

Size in proportion to the room and container (flowers 1½ times the height of the vase); balance (not top-heavy or lopsided); rhythm (the eye should travel easily around, by repeating shape, colour and texture and arranging at different heights); graded sizes from full-bloom to buds; stem ends close together; the plant material more important than the vase; not too many different colours (use small dull flowers with bright ones); emphasise twig shapes with space around each flower; harmony of flowers, leaves and vase.

Rangoli or alpana: traditional floor decoration on doorsteps, courtyards and verandahs with colours, flower petals, rice or maida powder. Tips: select the design to suit the festival or occasion, draw in double lines to fill between, ensure uniformity and balance, use contrasting colours next to each other, use a scale to neaten outlines, fill evenly and press flat, and fill the background so the design looks part of the floor. Coloured sawdust: sieve sawdust, mix 30 g dyeing colour in half a glass of water, dry in shade and store in plastic bags. Accessories: hang paintings according to wall size (a group of small paintings fitted in an imaginary square or rectangle), use spot lights, hang straight and even, harmonise lamp colours with the décor, place cushions randomly for colour, do not crowd curios and group similar materials together.
